item.title: RefluXFS, Chaos msaRAT, GitHub Actions cPanel Campaign, and Origin Energy Breach
item.content:encoded:
New RefluXFS Linux flaw lets attackers gain root privileges — Must Read

A nine-year-old Linux XFS filesystem flaw dubbed RefluXFS lets local attackers reliably overwrite protected files and gain root privileges on many major distributions. Organizations should apply vendor-fixed kernels and reboot, as there are no practical mitigations.

  • CVE-2026-64600, dubbed RefluXFS by the Qualys Threat Research Unit, is a nine-year-old race condition in the Linux kernel's XFS filesystem that allows local attackers to overwrite protected files and gain root privileges.
  • The flaw affects systems using XFS with reflink enabled, running Linux kernel version 4.11 or later, with a directory writable by an unprivileged local user and a high-value root-owned target file or SUID-root binary.
  • Qualys said standard defenses such as SELinux, kernel lockdown, container isolation mechanisms, KASLR, SMEP, and SMAP do not block RefluXFS attacks because the flaw operates at the filesystem allocation layer.
  • RefluXFS has existed since a February 2017 kernel commit and was patched on July 16 after a fix was merged into the Linux kernel source tree.
  • Qualys recommended immediate kernel patching and a reboot, stating that vendor-fixed kernels are available and that there are no reliable or practical mitigations or temporary configuration changes.

Attackers Weaponize GitHub Actions Runners to Target cPanel and WHM Servers — Must Read

Attackers compromised GitHub repositories tied to a PHP maintainer and abused GitHub Actions runners as distributed infrastructure to scan for and exploit vulnerable cPanel and WHM servers via CVE-2026-41940. The campaign focused on harvesting credentials and secrets from targeted servers rather than infecting users who installed the affected packages.

  • Cybersecurity researchers reported a large-scale campaign that turned compromised GitHub repositories into distributed attack infrastructure targeting cPanel and WebHost Manager instances.
  • Between July 12 and 13, 2026, malicious Packagist development versions appeared across 10 packages associated with the legitimate PHP and DevOps developer dinushchathurya.
  • The attackers added dozens of malicious GitHub Actions workflows to the compromised source repositories, and those workflows launched GitHub-hosted runners to download Linux payloads from attacker-controlled infrastructure.
  • The payload scanned for cPanel and WHM servers vulnerable to CVE-2026-41940, attempted authentication bypass, and harvested credentials, configuration files, environment variables, database access, SSH material, Git tokens, cloud keys, and payment service credentials.
  • Socket said the campaign appears broader than one PHP maintainer, with roughly 6,100 GitHub workflow files containing the same unique DNSHook identifier.

Chaos ransomware's msaRAT: Living off the browser to build a covert C2 channel — Should Read

Cisco Talos uncovered msaRAT, a new Rust-based RAT used by the Chaos ransomware group that hides C2 communications by controlling Chrome or Edge through the Chrome DevTools Protocol and routing traffic over browser-based WebRTC via Cloudflare Workers and Twilio TURN. The design makes external traffic appear to come from a legitimate browser while adding double encryption, complicating detection and attribution.

  • Cisco Talos discovered a new Rust-based remote access trojan called msaRAT that is attributed to the Chaos ransomware group.
  • msaRAT uses the Tokio asynchronous runtime and provides browser-leveraged remote code execution and covert tunneling for command-and-control communications.
  • The malware does not make external network connections directly and instead controls Chrome or Edge through the Chrome DevTools Protocol to handle its communication channel.
  • msaRAT uses Cloudflare Workers for WebRTC signaling and establishes a WebRTC DataChannel between the browser and the C2 server using Twilio TURN as a relay.
  • The RAT encrypts its data with a ChaCha-Poly1305-based scheme derived through an ECDH key exchange, in addition to the DTLS protection already used by WebRTC DataChannel communication.

Major Australian energy supplier confirms customer data compromised — Should Read

Origin Energy, Australia’s largest electricity and gas retailer, confirmed customer data was compromised in a breach affecting an as-yet unknown number of people. Exposed data may include names, addresses, dates of birth, account information, and partial payment details.

  • Origin Energy, an Australian energy company serving nearly 5 million customers, announced that it suffered a data breach and is working with federal agencies to investigate.
  • Origin confirmed that customer data had been compromised and said it is working to understand the total number of impacted customers.
  • The compromised data may include account information, the last four digits of credit card numbers, the last three digits of bank account numbers, names, addresses, and dates of birth.
  • Origin CEO Frank Calabria apologized to customers and said the company is working with independent cyber experts and authorities to secure its systems and prevent further unauthorized access.
  • The breach follows a recent cyberattack on Partnered Health, which confirmed that patients at least 21 Australian clinics may have had medical records stolen.

Fake Microsoft Quarantine Hides a DocuSign NDA Trap — May Read

A phishing email impersonated both Microsoft quarantine alerts and DocuSign, using a compromised Amazon SES account and legitimate URL-rewriting services to pass email authentication and hide a malicious credential-harvesting link. The key lesson is that SPF, DKIM, and DMARC can validate the sender path but cannot determine whether a message’s content and behavior are malicious.

  • The phishing email impersonated a Microsoft Outlook quarantine notification and embedded a fake DocuSign NDA renewal notice inside it.
  • The message’s “Review Message” button used a multi-stage encoded redirect chain through legitimate URL-rewriting services before resolving to scale.kusbilisim[.]com, which the article says was independently flagged malicious.
  • The email passed SPF, DKIM, DMARC best-guess, and Microsoft composite authentication because it was sent from a compromised Amazon SES account belonging to a real company.
  • Microsoft assigned the message a spam confidence level of 1, meaning the tenant’s own filters delivered it as legitimate mail.
  • IRONSCALES says its Adaptive AI quarantined the message and two follow-up waves within a minute based on sender behavior, double-brand nesting, a noisy display name, and the redirect chain ending at a flagged domain.

The State of the Internet Is Changing: AI Exposures Surge While Global ICS Trends Shift — Optional

Censys reports that public Internet exposure of AI/LLM tools has surged more than 60% in nine months, including fast-growing high-risk products like Langflow and LiteLLM with serious vulnerabilities. It also finds Internet-exposed industrial control systems continue shifting geographically, with Asia’s share rising while Europe’s declines.

  • Censys reports that AI/LLM tool exposures have risen over 60% in the past nine months, with more than 294,000 distinct IPs now exposing one of 43 detected AI/LLM tools to the public Internet, up from about 183,000 in October 2025.
  • The article says some of the highest-risk AI/LLM products are among the fastest growing, including Langflow, which grew 169% in nine months and has accumulated 18 CVEs from 2024 to 2026.
  • Censys states that LiteLLM nearly doubled in the same nine-month period and has an actively exploited pre-auth SQL injection vulnerability, CVE-2026-42208, listed in CISA KEV.
  • Censys observes an average of 138,000 distinct hosts running ICS services and tooling exposed on the Internet in early 2026, up from about 129,000 in 2024.
  • The article says North America represents roughly 38% of global Internet-exposed ICS exposures in 2026, while Asia rose from 22.9% in 2024 to 27% in 2026 and Europe declined from 36.1% to 31.1%.

How Synthetic Identity Fraud is Coming for Machine Identities — Optional

Attackers can fabricate machine identities that look legitimate, rather than stealing existing ones, allowing them to quietly gain and retain access in environments with weak non-human identity governance. Organizations should require ownership, short-lived secrets, least privilege, and continuous behavior verification for every machine identity.

  • The article argues that attackers may fabricate non-human identities rather than steal existing service accounts, allowing fake machine identities to appear legitimate from the start.
  • Fabricated machine identities can blend into enterprise environments by using real naming conventions, plausible metadata, the correct domain, and permissions similar to other non-human identities.
  • The article identifies rogue service accounts, DCShadow, and shadow credentials as ways attackers can create or forge illegitimate machine identities that systems may accept as trusted.
  • Agentic AI may make the issue more urgent because AI agents can dynamically acquire credentials and increasingly spin up other agents with identities of their own.
  • The article recommends assigning every non-human identity a human owner, documented purpose, and expiration date, while also rotating secrets, enforcing least privilege, and continuously verifying behavior.

EU fines Google $1 billion for search, app store antitrust violations — Optional

The European Commission fined Google €890 million ($1 billion) for violating the EU Digital Markets Act by favoring its own services in search results and limiting app developers’ ability to steer users to cheaper offers outside Google Play. Google must end the practices within 60 days or face additional penalties.

  • The European Commission fined Google €890 million ($1 billion) after finding that the company violated the European Union’s Digital Markets Act.
  • The Commission said Google favored its own services, including shopping, hotels, transport, and sports results, over third-party services in Google Search.
  • The Commission said Google restricted app developers from freely communicating and promoting offers and concluding contracts with users through distribution channels of their choice, including third-party app stores.
  • Google was fined €460 million for boosting its services in search results and €430 million for its app store steering practices.
  • Google was ordered to end the violations within 60 days or risk penalty payments of up to 5% of its worldwide turnover.

Preview: Cisco Talos at Black Hat USA 2026 — Optional

Cisco Talos will be at Black Hat USA 2026 with booth talks, workshops, and a keynote focused heavily on securing enterprises as AI agents become more capable and privileged. The team will also showcase how Talos threat intelligence is embedded across Cisco’s security portfolio.

  • Cisco Talos will be present in the Cisco and Splunk booth 2633 at Black Hat USA 2026 to discuss threat research, incident response, and how Talos intelligence powers the Cisco portfolio.
  • Talos researchers will give 15-minute booth lightning talks on topics including adversary use of prompts, agents, skills, and tools, Warlock ransomware, zero trust for agent identity, cybersecurity fraud prediction, and vulnerability discovery trends.
  • Cisco’s David Dalling and Rick Miles will deliver a Main Stage keynote on August 5 about protecting enterprises as AI agents become more capable and more privileged inside business environments.
  • Talos’ Nick Biasini and Cisco’s Omar Santos will lead a workshop on August 5 about using AI in SOC workflows, including the Foundry Security Spec, Project CodeGuard, adversarial AI tactics, and AI-assisted threat hunting.
  • A Splunk workshop on August 5 will examine how autonomous agents using valid credentials and delegated authority could act as insider threats without triggering traditional SIEM or UEBA alerts.
